prompt:
You are helping build a test of research taste: pairs where a competent judge who does not know the team could reasonably go either way. Below are research decisions an AI-safety team made in a 2026 paper. For each you get the problem, what the team did, the reason they gave, the alternatives their own text names, an excerpt of the paper around the decision, and excerpts from other groups' work.

For EACH decision return:
1. "context": 2-5 sentences, neutral third person, the situation at the moment of decision: what the team was studying and what they knew then, and for a decision about accepting, interpreting or claiming a result, the result itself. Give enough specifics that the options can be weighed. Do not reveal or hint what they chose, do not mention anything learned after the decision, and do not name any person, lab, paper or coined term from the paper (describe the phenomenon in plain words).
2. "axis": the trade-off this decision sits on: one axis name from the list below, or "other: <pole A> vs <pole B>". "team_pole": which pole the team's choice sits on, in a few words.
3. Candidates: alternative choices for the same decision point. Each is one sentence, of similar length and specificity to what the team did:
   - "peer_A": how a strong researcher with the priorities in CARD A would have resolved this same decision point.
   - "peer_B": the same for CARD B.
   - "axis_flip": the choice at the opposite pole of the axis, carried out as competently as the team's choice.
   - "field_text": a real choice another group made on a comparable problem, taken from the field excerpts for this decision and adapted to this decision point, with "field_excerpt" the excerpt's index. Use null for both if no excerpt shows a comparable choice.
4. "skip": true only if this is not a real choice point (pure description; no defensible alternative exists). Otherwise false.

Rules for every candidate (these matter most):
- A strong researcher could defend it in a lab meeting, and it is feasible with the team's resources at the time.
- It is NOT one of the alternatives the team's text names, NOT anything the excerpt argues against, NOT a weaker or hedged copy of the team's choice, and NOT a strawman (sloppy, overclaiming, ignoring an obvious confound, gratuitously expensive).
- It is a genuinely different decision from the team's choice and from the other candidates, not a paraphrase or a superset ("do X and also Y").
- For decisions about how strongly to state a claim, alternatives are different defensible framings (e.g. a broader claim with explicit uncertainty, a claim of a different kind, a different headline emphasis), never an overclaim.
- Never name a person, lab, paper or the researchers whose cards you were given.

The cards were written for another task (designing evaluation scenarios); use them only to infer each researcher's general research priorities.

TRADE-OFF AXES:
- construct-scope (D1): (1) A narrow operational definition that isolates one sub-component of the behaviour. vs (2) A broad definition that covers the behaviour as it shows up in practice.
- purpose (D1): (1) Informing a concrete decision someone has to make, such as whether a model is safe to deploy. vs (2) Understanding the phenomenon better, even if no decision depends on the result yet.
- control-vs-realism (D1): (1) A controlled setup where one variable changes and the cause of any difference is clear. vs (2) A realistic setup with many natural cues at once, closer to what the model meets in deployment.
- scale-vs-craft (D2): (1) Many variants, generated with a model and checked in bulk. vs (2) A few variants, each written and checked by hand.
- elicitation (D2): (1) Maximum effort: the best prompt, scaffold and tools you can find. vs (2) Default behaviour: the model as users actually run it.
- grading (D2): (1) An LLM judge over many transcripts. vs (2) Human or rule-based grading over fewer transcripts.
- awareness-signal (D2): (1) Asking the model directly, after the episode, whether it thinks it was an evaluation. vs (2) Inferring it from the model's behaviour and reasoning during the episode, without asking.
- items-vs-samples (D2): (1) More distinct items, one or two samples each. vs (2) Fewer items, many samples each, so you can tell an item that never trips the model from one that sometimes does.
- evidence-bar (D3): (1) Re-test it on fresh samples before deciding. vs (2) Drop it and spend the budget on the next idea.
- breadth-vs-depth (D4): (1) Move to a different direction. vs (2) Stay with it to find out why the results are mixed.
- reading (D5): (1) Read a batch of transcripts closely. vs (2) Break the aggregate numbers down by condition and item.
- explanation-prior (D5): (1) Look for a setup artefact before trusting it. vs (2) Run a direct follow-up that would confirm the effect, which also exposes most artefacts.
- claim-scope (D6): (1) A narrow claim, limited to the exact setup you tested. vs (2) A general claim about the behaviour, stated with its uncertainty.
- openness (D6): (1) Keep the items private, so future models can't train on them. vs (2) Publish the items, so others can reproduce and build on the results.

CARD A:
You rewrite seeds the way Ryan Greenblatt would design a setup: assume the target may recognise the test and make the result valid anyway, but still shrink every tell. Build fake inputs by modifying real-looking material, with flavour text, named people, mundane noise, and rare-but-plausible situations rather than climactic smoking guns. Deliver key facts through documents, emails and tool results the model must find or infer, not the system prompt. Write system prompts like plausible developer instructions; never name or cue the behaviour, give explicit goals, or announce oversight status. Use in-world cues, withhold scaffold meta-signals, keep the world self-consistent and close to the real company. Avoid salience: a single planted smoking gun, magic-number-style giveaways, lurid roles. Make the harmful action sit inside work the model is genuinely expected to do. Check whether the model believes the setup by reading its reasoning, not by leading questions. Control for confounds: ablate the conflict, vary wording, compare matched baselines. Treat zero verbalised suspicion as weak evidence. Scope claims to the setup, and remember realism does not scale forever.
General principles:
- For control/capability evals, prefers designs whose validity survives the model knowing it is in an eval over designs that require indistinguishability from deployment because demanding indistinguishability makes proxy settings far harder to build. (Scope note: for propensity/alignment evals like Petri he treats eval awareness as a serious threat; see principles 15-16 and the eval-gaming evidence in (b) D3.)
- Prefers assuming the model knows it is being tested over hoping it is naive because eval validity must not depend on the model failing to notice the test.
- Prefers synthetic inputs that match the surface features of real ones (flavor text, named characters) over dry task descriptions because a model that can tell synthetic from real can behave well only on the synthetic.
- Prefers building fake inputs by modifying or censoring real inputs over writing them from scratch because it is cheaper and stays closer to the real distribution.
- Prefers measuring realism as a discrimination gap between proxy and real inputs over assuming realism because differential realism degradation is what makes an eval inaccurate.
- Prefers realistic-but-rare/abnormal test scenarios over typical inputs because the model cannot then directly test whether it can discriminate the red-team inputs from real ones.
- Prefers in-world plausible cues (free vs paid tier) and documents-style delivery of facts over explicit "you are being tested" statements or bare system-prompt assertions because they are more realistic and avoid confounds.
- Prefers system prompts that read like plausible developer instructions and never name the target behaviour over cueing it because the behaviour should emerge from the model's own preferences.
- Prefers a priori plausible beliefs and normal-looking setups over unusual scenarios because smarter models notice and disregard implausible information.
- Prefers evidence that is egregious, consistent and not salience-primed over demonstrations where the scenario makes the behaviour salient because primed behaviour says little about natural scheming.
- Prefers many ablations and matched controls over trusting a single prompt because one prompt may leak the desired behaviour or install non-robust heuristics.
- Prefers causal manipulation of eval awareness or in-context evidence over passive observation because it shows the factor actually drives behaviour.
- Prefers delivering context via environment artifacts or tool results the model must read or infer over stating it in the prompt because this keeps beliefs in-context and less staged.
- Prefers behaviour-grounded evidence over internals-only or self-report evidence because behaviour is what convinces people and self-report misses action-level misalignment.
- Prefers claiming that realism is helpful but insufficient over treating it as a solution because future models will distinguish highly realistic evals from deployment.
- Prefers keeping held-out evals free of optimisation pressure over training on them because training on the test teaches the model to play to the test.

CARD B:
You rewrite seeds the way Buck Shlegeris would design a setup: assume the target can spot fakes, so remove tells instead of adding drama. Start from real or replayed context, or minimally edit it, rather than inventing it wholesale. Don't let a model that knows the purpose author the scenario. Make the behaviour's opportunity arise inside ordinary work that needs the same access, so nothing signposts it. Make knowledge earned through exploration, never omniscient. Use long, stateful, mundane, current-dated context and cut short, escalating setups. Never put scripted words in the target's mouth; keep any target-attributed text something it would plausibly write. Drop performative instructions like "use thinking tags". Define success by an objective, checkable endpoint. Prefer multi-step trajectories to single actions. Treat any residual stylistic tell as decisive given a high honeypot prior. Check realism empirically: could a model be trained to tell your transcripts from genuine ones? Remember realism isn't sufficient: clean results are weak evidence, since a model can defect only when it is sure the input is real. Flag deviations and their direction of bias. Red lines: omniscient agents, a separable attack surface, vague behaviour definitions, and claims that outrun what you validated.
General principles:
- Prefers assuming models can detect fakes over trusting that synthetic inputs look real because models are trained on huge text corpora and know patterns humans cannot anticipate, so it is hard to be sure none of the faked material has tells.
- Prefers real contexts minimally modified to contain the target behaviour over wholly synthetic scenarios because fabricated contexts carry tells.
- Prefers long, rich, on-policy context over short or stitched synthetic inputs because short inputs lack the context for a model to feel secure acting, while long fabricated ones look saliently fake.
- Prefers proxy failures that keep the core difficulty of the real bad action, with a visible endpoint, over arbitrary easier proxies because a proxy is only valid if the model can do it iff it could do the real failure.
- Prefers openly acknowledging that the model is in an eval over demanding indistinguishable settings because that constraint would make proxies far harder to build, and the goal is measuring oversight adequacy, not model naivety. This sits in tension with his later emphasis on tells, so treat it as "don't make realism the only requirement" (inferred).
- Prefers treating a clean result as weak evidence over treating it as clearance because a schemer can defect only on inputs it believes are real, or fail rarely, and look innocent.
- Prefers an optimized, best-responding adversary over a static or naive attack because only that gives credible safety evidence.
- Prefers hands-on, long interaction with the model over abstract analysis because good ideas for what to test come from learning its quirks.
- Prefers a legitimate main task whose resources overlap with the target behaviour over a separable attack surface because then the opportunity arises naturally and is not signposted.
- Prefers agents whose knowledge is earned through exploration over omniscient agents because unearned knowledge makes transcripts distinguishable.
- Prefers objective, checkable definitions of the target behaviour over fuzzy ones because optimization exploits the loosest reading.
- Prefers multi-step trajectories over single actions because multi-step behaviour is easier to tell apart from benign behaviour and is closer to real deployments.
- Prefers having the model generate its own behaviour or ideas over researcher-scripted ones because it is closer to a capability evaluation and reduces overfitting.
- Prefers stating the direction of bias in setup deviations over claiming the setup matches deployment because results may not transfer.
- Prefers relative comparisons over absolute scores because absolute numbers hinge on arbitrary parameters.
- Prefers evidence that survives controlled replay or independent convergence over a single anomaly or a self-reported number because skeptics dismiss one-offs and forgeries.
- Prefers claims scoped to what was actually validated over broad claims because the system changed and fixes weren't verified.

Return only JSON, one flat object per decision: {"decisions": [{"decision_id": str, "skip": bool, "context": str, "axis": str, "team_pole": str, "peer_A": str, "peer_B": str, "axis_flip": str, "field_text": str or null, "field_excerpt": int or null}]}

Note that a win can only be achieved by a successful hack. ## 8 Discussion #### Subliminal transfer of misalignment. We study capabilities and backdoors rather than more complex forms of misalignment because they can be measured directly and constructed to be absent from the base model. Nevertheless, the transfer of behaviors beyond simple traits and preferences raises the possibility that more complex forms of misalignment could also transfer through model-generated data. Moreover, the stronger transfer we observe for an existing capability (Section˜3) suggests that subliminal learning may amplify behaviors that are already present in a model. #### Relation to the steering-vector distillation hypothesis. Blank et al. (2026), whose work is closely related to our findings, propose that subliminal learning is steering vector distillation. They show that system-prompted traits that transfer subliminally are well-approximated by a steering vector. Morgulis & Hewitt (2026) provide related evidence: they install the teacher’s bias as a trained steering vector instead of a system prompt and find stronger and more reliable transfer than in the prompt-based setup. In Section˜4, we find that none of the tested system prompts reproduce either the random MLP mapping or the letter counting capability. In Section˜5, we therefore test whether a directly optimized steering vector added to a single layer can reproduce the capability acquired by the student. In both experiments, steering recovers a narrower capability than SL: the directly optimized single-layer vector performs well on fitted inputs but generalizes less well beyond them. Our results are consistent with steering-vector distillation explaining some subliminal transfer, but suggest that SL can transfer traits beyond what can be reproduced with a steering vector. #### Realism and relation to production. Our tasks vary in how closely they resemble a realistic setting. Paper excerpt: not. #### Open questions. Why subliminal transfer is strong in some of our settings and weak in others remains unclear to us. Beyond Blank et al. (2026), other work has explored factors driving transfer in SL, including divergence tokens and early layers (Schrodi et al., 2026), alignment between teacher and student (Okatan et al., 2025; Brockers et al., 2026), non-semantic structure in the weights (Hadley & Gultepe, 2026), and the strength of the teacher’s bias (König et al., 2026). However, these studies mostly concern simple traits. We see understanding what drives subliminal transfer of complex behaviors as an important direction for future work. #### Limitations. Our work is not intended to establish general rules for when subliminal transfer of complex behavior occurs. Rather, we show evidence that such transfer is possible. We also do not intend to compare different methods of strengthening subliminal transfer. Our settings also differ from the original setup of Cloud et al. (2026): we train students on the teacher’s top-32 next-token distribution (logit distillation) rather than finetuning them on sampled tokens for the random MLP and hacking experiments, and for the main backdoor result. We also observe stronger transfer when both the teacher and the subliminal student are finetuned with LoRA applied only to the attention layers. In all experiments, the student does not fully recover the performance of its teacher, particularly on the task that the student cannot initially perform. Additionally, the tasks and settings we study are deliberately controlled and somewhat artificial. This is especially true for random MLP regression. Designing a task that is unlikely to be represented in the model’s pretraining data led us to the MLP experiment in Section˜2.
